newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs lay low as Croats gear up for crucial vote.
newsitem.headline: Serbs lay low as Croats gear up for crucial vote.

text.p: Croatia is about to hold regional and municipal elections setting the stage for the reintegration of its last Serb enclave, but the war-wrecked region looks more divorced from the rest of the country than ever.
The countrywide voting set for April 13 will include Eastern Slavonia for the first time since Croatia proclaimed independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991.

Minority Serbs carved out three enclaves in a revolt against Croatian statehood. After Croatian troops easily recaptured two in 1995, the Serbs agreed to "peaceful reintegration" of the third, Eastern Slavonia.
But only 10 days before the polls, Eastern Slavonia, now secured by 5,000 U.N. peace troops, bears little sign of the pre-election activity sweeping the rest of Croatia.

Eastern Slavonia remains grey, barren and battered from war, devoid of high-tech, nouveau-riche luxury that has sprung up on the other side of truce lines guarded by U.N. transitional (UNTAES) forces and joint Croat-Serb police.

Instead, a handful of desperate Serbs, mostly women, persist in daily rallies against reintegration in front of the UNTAES base in Vukovar, the area's main town all but demolished in a 1991 Serb siege along the banks of the Danube River.

The peaceful protests began in February with anti-Croat and anti-UNTAES slogans, demanding that the region remain a single county to preserve Serb autonomy rather than be divided into two units, both with Croat majorities.
But the protests had shrunk in size and scope of demands. "Now we have 200-300 demonstrators whereas in the beginning there were up to 1,000," UNTAES spokesman Philip Arnold said.
He said Serb demonstrators now were only seeking protective agreements between presidents Slobodan Milosevic of nearby Serbia and Franjo Tudjman of Croatia.
Local Serbs, whose number UNTAES puts at roughly 120,000, only barely met a generously extended deadline to register their candidates by midnight on Tuesday.
They merged all political factions, including moderate realists who back reintegration and diehard separatists, into a single bloc, the Independent Serb Democratic Party (SSDS).

The SSDS, which was to kick off its campaign with a low-key news conference on Thursday, faced numerous Croatian parties poised to soak up votes of the region's pre-1991 Croat majority, more than 80,000 of them war refugees.
Croatian parties have spent lavish amounts of time and money to promote themselves and each vow to best protect the interests of Croats returning to the region.
For security reasons, local campaigning has been confined primarily to promotional spots on Croatian state television.

Some Croatian opposition parties have appeared in the enclave without incident but an appearance by Tudjman's nationalist HDZ on Monday prompted a barrage of eggs and bricks from Serb nationalist protesters.
Unlike the Serbs, Croats have no doubts that reintegration will take place to their advantage only, as soon as the UNTAES mandate expires or is considerably downsized, on July 15.
The HDZ has appealed to returning Croats to set aside feelings of revenge and live peacefully with Serb neighbours.
But the HDZ has also encouraged them not to disperse votes among too many parties to avoid giving the Serbs a theoretical chance of winning majorities in some smaller towns.

"We are now confronted with Serbs united in a single electoral body who will try to bite off as big a slice of power as possible," Branimir Glavas, HDZ leader in Osijek, a city on the Croatian side of the truce line, told a rally on Wednesday.
U.N. officials said the number of Serb applicants for voting papers rose 30 percent in the week before the April 5 deadline.
